claims.claim: Studies of Aristotle's phantasia have been one-sided by prioritizing its role in explaining delusions, hallucinations, dreams, and memory while neglecting its role in action explanation.
claims.ground: Critics use DA III.3 and Parva Naturalia as main texts and treat action-related passages in DA III.9-11 and De Motu as parasitic and of smaller philosophical interest.
claims.warrant: A comprehensive understanding of phantasia requires equal attention to all contexts in which Aristotle employs the concept.
claims.rebuttal: Freudenthal claims that discussion of phantasia in action contexts would require elaboration disproportionate to the importance of the subject.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Understanding phantasia's role in action contexts is crucial for analyzing Aristotle's theory of action.
claims.ground: Phantasia and desire are jointly necessary conditions for animal motion, and phantasia is a necessary condition for desire, which must prepare desire before action can occur.
claims.warrant: If phantasia is necessary for the causal chain leading to action, understanding it is indispensable for understanding action itself.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: It is methodologically unsound to assume that 'decaying-sense' passages should illuminate action contexts but not vice versa.
claims.ground: Action contexts are equally valuable evidence of Aristotle's interests and views regarding phantasia.
claims.warrant: All textual evidence should be weighted equally unless there are specific grounds for privileging some passages over others.
claims.rebuttal: The standard approach assumes decaying-sense passages are foundational for understanding all uses of phantasia.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's account of phantasia is closely tied to his usage of phainesthai (appear) and reflects a general interest in how things appear to living creatures.
claims.ground: Aristotle uses phainesthai and related words in analyzing a wide range of experiences, and phantasia plays a central role in both delusion/memory contexts and motivation contexts.
claims.warrant: The semantic connection between phantasia and phainesthai suggests the faculty concerns appearance broadly, not just specific phenomena.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: There is no canonical theory of phantasia in Aristotle, but rather assorted observations that are sometimes apparently inconsistent.
claims.ground: Even the detailed exposition in DA III.3 is internally inconsistent on important points.
claims.warrant: If the most detailed treatment is inconsistent, there cannot be a single unified theory underlying all uses of the term.
claims.rebuttal: The standard view treats DA III.3 as the key to all other uses of phantasia in Aristotle.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Only Aristotle's basic interest in appearing, not the decaying-sense theory, can explain the extended role ascribed to phantasia in action contexts.
claims.ground: The decaying-sense theory from DA III.3 and Parva Naturalia cannot account for phantasia's operation in action explanation.
claims.warrant: A theory adequate to action contexts must accommodate phantasia's concurrent operation with perception in the presence of objects, which decaying-sense cannot do.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The prevalent view interprets Aristotelian phantasmata as mental images that resemble what they represent and are contemplated as internal pictures.
claims.ground: Aristotle's claims that all thinking requires phantasmata are usually interpreted to mean thinking requires such internal pictorial objects as raw material.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: There is much less evidence for the image-view of phantasia than has usually been supposed.
claims.ground: The clear connection of phantasia and phantasmata with pictorial representative images is limited to a few passages in DA and Parva Naturalia concerning decaying sense; many passages make better sense emphasizing connection with phainesthai, and some make no sense at all with images.
claims.warrant: If images are only clearly present in a few passages and problematic or unnecessary in others, they cannot be central to the theory.
claims.rebuttal: The prevalent view assumes images are central to Aristotle's theory of phantasia.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The extension of phantasia's role in action contexts to operations concurrent with perception and in the presence of objects is especially hard to explain using images as interpretive key.
claims.warrant: Mental images paradigmatically represent absent objects, so a theory based on images struggles to explain phantasia's role when objects are present.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The prevalence of the image view of phantasia can be explained by the prevalence of the empiricist view of imagination.
claims.ground: Many Aristotle scholars appeared unable to conceive of alternatives to the empiricist interpretation except the clearly false view that phantasia is a kind of propositional judgment.
claims.warrant: When scholars assume a dichotomy between only two interpretive options and find one satisfactory, they will extend it beyond its evidential base.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The empiricist image theory makes two basic claims: (1) imagination always involves images that represent in virtue of similarity, and (2) imagination always involves two logically distinct processes—having an image and inspecting it.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The two claims of image theory are logically independent.
claims.ground: One might hold that images must be similar without granting there is more to be found in them than was intentionally put there, or insist on picture-like density while allowing conventional representation.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Objections to image theory based on the ontological status of images (what sort of entity, in what space) are not compelling.
claims.ground: Accounting for images within a physicalist picture of mind is no more difficult in principle than accounting for sensations, and the location problem for images is analogous to the familiar problem about where sensations are located.
claims.warrant: If two problems are structurally analogous and one is tractable, the other should be tractable by the same methods.
claims.rebuttal: Some object that non-physical objects cannot have dimensions or location
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Similarity is neither necessary nor sufficient for pictorial representation.
claims.ground: An object closely resembles but does not represent a copy of itself; conversely, reference can be secured independently of resemblance, as when a fish symbolizes Christ or a bird symbolizes the Holy Spirit.
claims.warrant: Representation is a type of reference or denotation, which requires more than mere resemblance.
claims.rebuttal: Image theory assumes similarity is both necessary and sufficient for representation
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The assumption that there is one 'innocent' or pure way of seeing an object is a myth.
claims.ground: Representing has always been more about interpreting than reproducing; we are always representing an object as something, never copying it in all the ways it is.
claims.warrant: If representation necessarily involves selection and interpretation, there can be no theory-neutral 'pure view' of an object.
claims.rebuttal: Image theory assumes there is one correct way of seeing/painting the object as it is
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Artistic representation can potentially enhance or alter our knowledge of the world and change how we see things.
claims.ground: We may develop an ability to see structures and relationships we were previously unaware of; as Picasso said of his portrait of Gertrude Stein that did not initially look like her, 'No matter; it will.'
claims.warrant: If representation involves interpretation rather than mere copying, it can introduce new ways of seeing that become validated over time.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's theory of phantasia attempts to avoid the passive picture of seeing embodied in the copy view of representation.
claims.ground: Although Aristotle occasionally makes superficial errors about representation, his most significant contribution is attempting to avoid the underlying error of the passive view of perception.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The image view wrongly implies that every image must have an actual referent in the world (no image has null denotation).
claims.ground: What we imagine may not correspond to anything actual; just as there are fictional pictures, there are fictional imaginings.
claims.warrant: A theory of representation must account for both actual and fictional reference.
claims.rebuttal: Image theory provides a simplistic view of pictorial reference that cannot handle fictions
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The 'problem of fictions' and 'problem of hallucinations' arise only because of more basic difficulties with image theory.
claims.ground: These need not be problems at all, as Dennett has pointed out.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Imagining need not involve anything like a picture.
claims.ground: Image theory persistently ignores auditory, olfactory, and tactile images and has no account showing they function like visual picture-images.
claims.rebuttal: Image theory focuses exclusively on visual pictorial imagination
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Many cases of imagining involve symbolic resemblance that is not representational but descriptional.
claims.ground: One might imagine music by picturing the score, books by thinking of Library of Congress numbers, or Valhalla by thinking of its Wagnerian leitmotif.
claims.warrant: If the symbolic relationship is not informationally dense and does not support pictorial exploration, it is descriptional rather than representational.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In many cases of imagining, there is never more content than what the imaginer intentionally put in.
claims.ground: Sartre, Ishiguro, and possibly Wittgenstein claim imagining is like sketching without stepping back to see what one has made; an image has just the content with which we invest it.
claims.rebuttal: This denial that we ever get new information from imagining seems excessively rigid
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Even where imagining yields new information, the analogy to looking at a picture is seldom perfect.
claims.ground: Much imagining is more diagrammatic than pictorial (some features are dismissed as contingent), and some information that would be required in a picture may be left unspecified.
claims.warrant: If imagining rarely involves objects that are both dense and replete, it differs structurally from pictorial representation.
claims.rebuttal: The pure picture-view claims imagining always involves inspecting a dense representational object
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The image theory embodies a false distinction between copying and interpreting, which explains its neglect of the connection between imagining and our intentions.
claims.ground: The theory fails to account for the active, interpretive role of the imaginer.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Objections to the image theory of imagination apply with suitable adjustment to theories of perceptual awareness that rely centrally on images.
claims.ground: Even someone not moved to discard the image theory of imagination might find these objections telling against using images to explain thinking or perceiving.
claims.warrant: If the problems with images as explanations of imagination are structural, they will afflict any theory that uses images to explain mental phenomena.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The concept of 'what is seen by someone as F' forms the basis for Aristotle's discussions of awareness that leads to action.
claims.ground: Phantasia to someone is what is seen by them as F, connecting to how things appear to sentient beings.
claims.warrant: A broad interest in appearances to sentient beings underlies more specialized discussions of envisaging and action-awareness.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: We should determine the meaning of phantasia in context by maintaining awareness of its connection to phainesthai, finding images only where concretely evidenced.
claims.ground: A survey of uses before and in Aristotle shows this is the most fruitful interpretive approach.
claims.warrant: We should not assume Aristotle produces bad theory based on technical usage rather than subtler theory tied to ordinary usage.
claims.rebuttal: Against assuming phantasia always refers to picture-like internal objects.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's uses of phantasia vary across three contexts: picture-like internal objects, episodes of envisaging, and seeing X as F.
claims.ground: Understanding what questions Aristotle asks in each case determines what is in view.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In DA III and MA 6-8, Aristotle gives phantasia a central role in explaining why and how animals move towards goals, claiming it functions even when actual perceiving or thinking are occurring.
claims.ground: These contexts more explicitly than any others assign phantasia this central place.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The distinction-making faculties (kritika) including phantasia, aisthesis, and nous both present objects of desire to animals and present concrete situations as examples of what is desired or not.
claims.ground: MA 6 lists phantasia among faculties needed to explain animal motion, categorizing it with aisthesis and nous as kritika.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Any one of the three kritika can operate without the other two, combined with orexis, to produce action.
claims.ground: The sketchy account in MA 6 suggests desire + sense-perception or desire + thinking would suffice to move the animal without phantasia involvement.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Despite initial suggestions of disjunctive operation, Aristotle later assigns phantasia a broader role as involved in every action.
claims.ground: At MA 701a18ff, phantasia prepares desire whether or not actual perceiving occurs, coming about through thought or sense-perception.
claims.rebuttal: Contrasts with earlier passages suggesting phantasia as one alternative among three faculties.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Motion always requires both phantasia and desire together.
claims.ground: DA 432b15 states motion occurs with both phantasia and orexis; 433b26-30 says animals cannot desire without phantasia.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: All phantasia is connected either with thinking or with perception, dividing into logistike and aisthesis-related types.
claims.ground: Both MA and DA accounts state phantasia comes about through thought or sense-perception.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Lower 'incomplete creatures' must possess both epithumia and some vague phantasia to explain their motion, not just aisthesis and epithumia alone.
claims.ground: DA III.11 discusses incomplete animals, concluding they must have phantasia since they move, though Aristotle grants this grudgingly.
claims.warrant: Aisthesis plus epithumia would be insufficient to explain motion without phantasia.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The deliberative phantasia (bouleutike) is the species peculiar to rational creatures, distinct from the general type.
claims.ground: DA III.11 distinguishes bouleutike phantasia and provides an example of its functioning.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia and aisthesis are 'the same' capacity but different in einai (being/essence).
claims.ground: DA 432a31 says phantasia's einai differs from other faculties but might be 'the same as' another; De Insomniis 459a15 explicitly identifies it as same as aisthesis but different in einai.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The 'sameness but different einai' relationship likely means activities can be described as exercises of either capacity depending on the aspect to which we attend, not merely that they share a base capacity.
claims.ground: Aristotle uses phantastikon and aisthetikon (capacities) rather than phantasia and aisthesis (activities); parallel passages use difference in einai for two-description cases like the road up/down.
claims.warrant: When Aristotle says capacities are 'the same,' he implies activities traceable to one could also be traced to the other under different descriptions.
claims.rebuttal: Against interpreting this as separate activities based on a single general power.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Three inferences follow from aisthetikon and phantastikon being the 'same' capacity: (1) all perceivers can have phantasia with same physiological apparatus; (2) many aisthesis activities can be viewed as phantasia activities; (3) using both terms provides new information about the disposition.
claims.ground: These follow from Aristotle's statement about sameness and difference in einai.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In pre-Aristotelian usage, phantasma refers to 'what appears' rather than to a mental image
claims.ground: Plato's Sophist uses phantasma to describe something seen from a bad angle that appears like the beautiful but isn't truly similar; Philebus and Symposium use phantazesthai for appearing without implying imaging
claims.warrant: If a term is used consistently to describe mere appearing without reference to mental representations, its core meaning is 'appearing' rather than 'imaging'
claims.rebuttal: The standard view that phantasma means 'image' in pre-Aristotelian texts
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasma in Plato can describe both sensory and non-sensory appearing
claims.ground: In Symposium 211a5ff., phantazesthai describes how the Form of Beauty appears, explicitly contrasted with how perceptible objects, arguments, or knowledge appear
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Pre-Aristotelian phantasia vocabulary is used simply as relatives of phainetai without implying any particular theory of imaging
claims.ground: The terms appear in diverse contexts (dreams, hallucinations, ordinary appearing) without being appropriated as technical terms for a specific theory
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Even when phantasma is used for dream-appearances, it need not designate a representative image
claims.ground: Republic 380d explains divine apparitions not as images appearing but as gods themselves appearing in changed form; Philebus 34a-b discusses memory without using phantasia cognates
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle bases his investigations of phantasia on its connection with phainetai rather than on imaging
claims.ground: Multiple Aristotelian passages use phantasia to indicate how a scene looks to a creature without reference to imaging
claims.rebuttal: The standard interpretation that Aristotle has a technical image-theory
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotelian phantasia remains closely linked to phainetai even in technical contexts
claims.ground: EN 1114a32ff. discusses how the end appears depending on character; EE 1235b25-29 contrasts phantasia with doxa as different ways things appear; Insomn. 460b19 describes the sun appearing one foot wide while belief opposes this phantasia
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia represents a single isolated impression, contrasted with doxa which is based on experience and reflection
claims.ground: EE passage contrasts phantasia with doxa as being in different parts of soul; EN VII contrasts following phantasia of particulars with following general belief
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's phantasia is as wide-ranging as his notion of phainomena, embracing far more than perceptual data
claims.ground: DA 402b22-24 uses phantasia broadly for how incidental attributes appear to us; Owen has argued phainomena embraces more than perception
claims.rebuttal: Bonitz's claim that different 'senses' of phantasia should be separated
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's interest in phantasia concerns how an object or state of affairs registers with a creature and what content it has for them
claims.ground: The range of passages shows concern with how things are interpreted by living creatures rather than with mental imagery
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Sensory phantasia for Aristotle ascribes potentially motivating content to an animal's perception
claims.ground: The animal who 'phantasizes' perceives an object as a thing of a certain sort that could become an object of pursuit or avoidance
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle is concerned with 'seeing as' - how moving creatures become aware of objects in ways that move them
claims.ground: Like Wittgenstein's 'echo of thought in sight' but extended to creatures lacking thought and experience
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In Metaphysics V.29, phantasia refers to the false impression resulting from dreams, not to dream-images themselves
claims.ground: Dream-images (enupnia) are distinguished from the phantasia that results from them; the passage says dreams are something but not what they give the impression of being
claims.rebuttal: The interpretation that phantasia me ontos means 'dream image of what is not'
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: A hypocrite creates false phantasia by presenting himself deceptively, not by producing mental pictures in others
claims.ground: Met. 1025a5ff. says a man is called false if he often gives others false impressions, comparing this to states of affairs that create false phantasia
claims.warrant: If phantasia meant mental pictures, we would absurdly have to say hypocrites paint pictures in others' minds rather than deceiving through words and deeds
claims.rebuttal: The image-theory interpretation of phantasia
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: No simple mechanism of images or traces can explain the complex range of phenomena Aristotle studies under phantasia
claims.ground: The decaying-sense account cannot explain how a hypocrite produces misleading impressions of moral character through complex social interactions
claims.rebuttal: The decaying-sense account of phantasia
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The sun appearing one foot across does not require a mental picture but refers to how it presents itself visually
claims.ground: Both Insomn. and DA 428b2-4 contrast how the sun appears with what we believe about its actual size
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle does not claim that phantasia in the sun-example involves internally measuring a picture of the sun.
claims.ground: The person's phantasia has the real sun as its object, and phantasia is the activity of seeing it as a certain size, not seeing an internal picture.
claims.warrant: If phantasia involved internal pictures that we measure, this would be unilluminating and unsupported by textual evidence.
claims.rebuttal: The view that phantasia involves internally measuring pictorial representations
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Judgment differs from phantasia in requiring experience and induction, though both have the real object as their target.
claims.ground: The sun passage contrasts phantasia (seeing the sun as a certain size) with judgment (which requires experience and induction).
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle invokes images to explain memory and dreaming specifically in connection with his physiological theory of decaying sense, not as part of general psychological doctrine.
claims.ground: Memory and dreaming are explained via images that are likenesses of things in the world, but this is tied to the theory of persisting kinēseis rather than broader psychological commitments.
claims.warrant: The exigencies of physiological theory, not psychological doctrine, drive the postulation of images.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The theory of memory uses kinēseis (motions) that persist after perception and act like signet-ring impressions of aisthēmata.
claims.ground: Aristotle likens these kinēseis to cloud forms that resemble different things and describes them as residual traces of actual aisthēsis that make impressions.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The expository passages on decaying sense use aisthēmata rather than phantasmata or phantasia, suggesting phantasia is not necessarily pictorial.
claims.ground: Although Mem. 451a15-16 uses phantasma for memory-image, the detailed theoretical passages discuss perceptual after-images with reference to aisthēmata, not phantasmata.
claims.warrant: If phantasia necessarily meant pictorial image, Aristotle would consistently use phantasma/phantasia in these theoretical passages.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle claims phantasia can work by means of images in some cases, but 'image' is not the meaning of phantasma.
claims.ground: The PN advances the theoretical claim that phantasia sometimes works through images (phantasma can be like a picture), but context determines usage, not a fixed meaning.
claims.warrant: Just as empiricists don't define 'think' as 'have an image' even when using image-theory, Aristotle doesn't define phantasma as image.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's memory theory may use resemblance as criterion of symbolization but still doesn't fully amount to a pictorial image-theory.
claims.ground: At 450a25ff the 'image' in isolation is either a theōrēma or phantasma (theōrēma unlikely to be pictorial), and at 451a1 a noēma contrasted with mnēmoneuma suggests memory can work through non-pictorial thoughts regarded as referring to the past.
claims.rebuttal: The full-blown image-theory interpretation of Aristotle's memory account
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: There is no implication in Aristotle's memory theory that images have the informational density or definiteness characteristic of pictures.
claims.ground: Nothing in the text implies we can keep going back to the image to find new information or that the image has definite pictorial properties.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In the MA (later than Mem.), Aristotle presents a theory of memory without images, describing it as awareness of things themselves as eidōla (shadows/no longer extant).
claims.ground: The MA refers to memory as awareness of pleasant and painful things in the world as shadows, suggesting a non-pictorial account.
claims.warrant: This represents memory not as awareness of pictures but as a temporally-shaped awareness of things themselves, along lines suggested by modern criticism of image-theories.
claims.rebuttal: The earlier image-based theory of memory
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: DA III.3 is usually but problematically taken as the canonical account of phantasia defining it via decaying-sense theory.
claims.ground: The final paragraph of III.3 explains delusion via kinēseis set up by perception that remain in absence of object and are 'similar' to actual perceptions, seemingly indicating resembling images.
claims.warrant: If we treat III.3's conclusion as canonical, we must find images in many passages where context alone wouldn't indicate them.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: DA III.3 cannot be coherently interpreted as building up to the decaying-sense discussion as definitive summary.
claims.ground: Earlier in III.3, phantasia is invoked to explain error in presence of object (sun-example), contrasted with doxa, said to be 'in our power' as active conjuring, and used to explain unclear perception of actual objects—none of which fit narrow decaying-sense theory.
claims.rebuttal: The interpretation that treats the decaying-sense passage as Aristotle's definitive theory
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The best interpretive approach is to allow Aristotelian phantasia broad scope rather than forcing all passages to fit the most technical one.
claims.ground: Aristotle directs attention to a wide variety of phenomena under phantasia without always clearly distinguishing them, and the decaying-sense analysis doesn't fit the entire discussion.
claims.warrant: We should recognize the diversity of phenomena rather than reading away inconsistencies or making everything fit one technical passage.
claims.rebuttal: The interpretive approach that privileges one technical passage and harmonizes all others with it
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The phrase kata metaphoran at DA 428a1-4 does not rule out general uses of phantasia connected with phainetai in favor of image-cases.
claims.ground: Aristotle uses kata metaphoran consistently to designate conscious shifts away from basic ordinary usage (examples: oxu for pitch, dunamis in mathematics, andreios for quasi-courageous), not to contrast technical with ordinary senses.
claims.warrant: It would be odd and contrary to Aristotle's usual procedure to call a word's basic ordinary use kata metaphoran.
claims.rebuttal: The standard interpretation that reads this passage as restricting phantasia to image-cases
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The kata metaphoran usage Aristotle brackets is phantasia meaning '(mere) show, ostentatiousness,' not the basic phainetai-related sense.
claims.ground: Phantasia acquired this transferred meaning by Aristotle's time (first in Herodotus VII.10.5, frequent in Polybius), and Aristotle himself uses it at Rhet. 1404a11 for 'mere show aimed at the audience.'
claims.warrant: This 'mere show' sense, unlike basic phainetai-related uses, can accurately be described as kata metaphoran and involves no reference to phantasmata.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Freudenthal correctly identified the transferred sense of phantasia as 'mere show,' though he missed the Rhetoric passage that strengthens this interpretation.
claims.ground: Freudenthal observed that phantasia meant 'pomp, ostentatiousness' by Aristotle's time, and the Rhetoric passage confirms Aristotle's awareness of this usage.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's basic interest in phantasia is in how things in the world appear to living creatures, what creatures see their objects as, not primarily in mental images.
claims.ground: In contexts analyzing delusion, dreaming, and memory, Aristotle speaks of phantasia and phantasmata, but evidence indicates his focus is on how objects appear to creatures.
claims.warrant: The central theoretical role of appearance-talk makes it more important than the occasional references to decaying-sense images.
claims.rebuttal: The image view that reads images into every passage and treats them as centrally important to Aristotle's theory
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: A more plausible account of phantasia's role in action and thinking can be produced without assuming mental images.
claims.ground: The image view does not seem centrally important enough to rob Aristotle's general observations of their broad interest.
claims.rebuttal: The image-based interpretation of phantasia in action contexts
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia and aisthesis are two aspects to be discerned in many perceptual activities, not separate activities.
claims.ground: The statement that phantasia and aisthesis were one but different in einai is best understood as claiming two aspects of perception.
claims.rebuttal: The view that phantasia picks out some activities of perceptual capacity while aisthesis picks out other quite separate activities
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia cannot be understood everywhere as picking out a process of decaying sense in the absence of actual perception.
claims.ground: The theory of action in both MA and DA strongly claims that even when aisthesis is going on, phantasia must also be mentioned in the explanation.
claims.warrant: If phantasia were only decaying sense without perception, it could not be required when perception is present.
claims.rebuttal: The decaying-sense doctrine as comprehensive explanation of all phantasia contexts
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia is the faculty in virtue of which the animal sees his object as an object of a certain sort, giving perception potentially motivating content.
claims.ground: The use of phantasia in action-contexts and its broad connection with phainetai throughout Aristotle suggest this interpretation.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aisthesis by itself is insufficient to present the object in a way that moves the animal to act; instead it must 'prepare' a phantasia which in turn 'prepares' the desire.
claims.ground: This must be explained against the background of Aristotle's theory of aisthesis to make the hypothesis convincing.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: DA III.3's contrast of phantasia with aisthesis must be used cautiously to explain action passages because Aristotle seems to be thinking primarily of phantasia in the absence of the perceptible object.
claims.ground: The statement that aisthesis but not phantasia is always going on (428b8-9) might indicate we have phantasia only when the object is not present.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The statement that aisthesis is always accurate but phantasia can be false emphasizes the mechanical, reproductive side of aisthesis in Aristotle's theory.
claims.ground: This contrast at DA 428a11-12 is clearly helpful for understanding phantasia's role.
claims.warrant: The mechanical character of aisthesis explains why a further faculty is needed.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aisthesis just is a bodily alteration under a different description, and Aristotle can pick out the physiological alterations that are its matter.
claims.ground: Multiple DA passages identify aisthesis with bodily alteration.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia is accompanied of necessity by some bodily change, but the nature of the alteration is much less evident than with aisthesis.
claims.ground: Aristotle infers from the fact that phantasia alone, in the object's absence, can result in motion that it must involve bodily change.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia works by presenting the animal with the form or essence of its object, which has an effect like that of the object itself.
claims.ground: Aristotle states this at MA 701b19ff and 703b19ff, calling the forms presented 'of the pleasant or painful' or 'of that which produces the affections'.
claims.warrant: Whereas in aisthesis the animal becomes just like the object, when phantasia is operative the animal becomes aware of the object as a thing of a certain sort.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Because of the passive character of Aristotelian aisthesis, a further faculty (phantasia) is required to explain the agent's selective fastening on certain aspects of his environment.
claims.ground: Initial examination of attempts to distinguish phantasia from aisthesis indicates this is why the special awareness of phantasia is important.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: It is because of the prevalence of the passive picture of aisthesis and Aristotle's belief that proper objects of senses are qualities not things, that he turns to phantasia to explain selective interpretation of environment.
claims.ground: The passive conception remains central in DA and PN despite some passages in DA II.5 ascribing more active, interpretive function to aisthesis.
claims.warrant: The passive picture is necessary in Aristotle's view to explain perceptual accuracy.
claims.rebuttal: Passages in DA II.5 that ascribe to aisthesis a more active, interpretive function
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In DA II.12, aisthesis receives perceptible forms without matter, like wax receiving the impress of a signet-ring without the metal.
claims.ground: Aristotle compares aisthesis to wax at DA 424a18-19, contrasting with plants that absorb matter.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aisthesis is affected by things that have color, taste, or sound not insofar as they are what each is spoken of as being, but insofar as they possess a certain quality.
claims.ground: Aristotle states this at DA 424b21ff to explain what aisthesis receives.
claims.warrant: The faculty plays an entirely passive role, receiving but not selecting.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: To be moved to action an animal has to become aware of something qua what-it-is-called (e.g., man as man), not just qua its perceptible quality (e.g., as pale).
claims.ground: When we perceive a rose by sight, it is the rose qua white that acts upon sight, not the rose qua rose; but action requires awareness of unified objects under descriptions.
claims.warrant: The forms presented by phantasia were forms of the pleasant and fearful, hence necessarily of things as unitary objects under some description.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: When we actively focus on some object in our environment, separating it from its context and seeing it as a certain thing, the faculty of phantasia or the phantasia-aspect of aisthesis is called into play.
claims.ground: We are always passively receiving perceptual stimuli, but active focusing requires something more than mere passive reception.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: It was in answer to problems growing out of his precise delimitation of aisthesis in DA II.12 that Aristotle turned increasingly to the faculty of phantasia in DA's account of perception's role in action.
claims.ground: Despite inconsistencies where aisthesis plays a more active part or phantasia is not mentioned where expected, this developmental pattern is reasonable to suppose.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In DA II.8, voice differs from mere noise because the striker must be a living creature with phantasia; voice is noise that is indicative (semantikos) of something.
claims.ground: Aristotle distinguishes voice from noise at DA 420b31ff by requiring phantasia.
claims.warrant: An animal's utterance conveys something only if it is about something, i.e., only if the animal is aware of something in virtue of phantasia.
claims.rebuttal: Hicks's interpretation that it is the presence of a mental image that differentiates vocal sound from noise
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Voice is semantikos of an object or state of affairs to which the animal has directed his attention, not of a mental picture.
claims.ground: On the image reading, voice would be semantikos of the mental picture, which is a bizarre claim without textual or philosophical backing.
claims.warrant: It is more plausible to see Aristotle as saying utterance conveys something only if the animal is aware of something in the world via phantasia.
claims.rebuttal: Hicks's view that voice is semantikos of an internal image
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The theory of phantasia helps Aristotle account for the interpretive side of perception.
claims.ground: The preceding analysis shows how phantasia enables selective, content-bearing awareness beyond passive sensory reception.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Reception and interpretation are not separable but thoroughly interdependent in perception.
claims.ground: Aisthesis and phantasia being 'the same faculty' implies there is no receptive 'innocent eye' in perception, and how something appears to me is bound up with my past, prejudices, and needs.
claims.warrant: If it is only through phantasia, not aisthesis alone, that one apprehends the object as an object, then there can be no uninterpreted view of it.
claims.qualifier: at least on the level of form or object-perception
claims.rebuttal: The view that there is a distinction between the given/received and the interpreted
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle still believes in the given to the extent that aisthesis presents uninterpreted colors and sounds.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia is the animal's awareness of some object or state of affairs that may prove to be an object of desire.
claims.ground: It can serve both to present the object of desire initially and to specify the object at hand as what is desired.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia can account for delusion in practical cases.
claims.ground: The example of a dog seeing ammonia solution as water or drink illustrates how phantasia presents objects incorrectly.
claims.warrant: The role of phantasia is the same in practical and non-practical cases; the difference lies solely in the role of desire.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia is not best analyzed as a disposition or tendency to treat an object as X, but as a psychological process.
claims.ground: A physiological description is always theoretically available for phantasia, and if we knew it, we could potentially determine the phantasia even in cases where no desire or behavior followed.
claims.warrant: Token-identity (not type-identity) between psychological and physiological descriptions means phantasiai are not logically dependent on resulting action.
claims.rebuttal: The view that phantasia should be analyzed as a disposition
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Animals generally just follow whatever presents itself to them as suitable because they cannot weigh one phantasia against another or correct one with judgment.
claims.ground: Animals cannot deliberate about which phantasia to pursue.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: There are two types of phantasia: deliberative (calculative) and perceptual.
claims.ground: The perceptual type belongs to other animals as well as humans, while deliberative phantasia involves looking to the future and weighing courses of action.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Deliberative phantasia involves measuring using a single criterion and making one phantasma out of many.
claims.ground: The agent must determine whether to do this or that through reasoning, seeking the greater good.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Ross's image-theory interpretation that deliberation involves combining pictorial elements is unfortunately crude and over-narrow.
claims.ground: It implies that whatever criterion one selects (goodness, bigness, beauty) must be susceptible of pictorial representation.
claims.rebuttal: Ross's collage view of deliberation
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Human deliberative phantasia enables seeing consequences as following from an action and measuring one set of consequences against another using some criterion.
claims.ground: Unlike animals who follow one phantasia after another sporadically, humans can look to the future and past experience, deliberating and weighing possible courses.
claims.warrant: Discrete considerations 'this or that' become the unity 'this rather than that.'
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Only humans have phantasia from inference (phantasian ek sullogismou), which enables deliberation.
claims.ground: Animals employ the structures revealed in the MA account of the syllogism but lack the ability to deliberate about results.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Deliberative phantasia can involve picturing or envisaging but need not be explained solely through pictorial images.
claims.ground: DA III.7 speaks of calculation using phantasmata or noemata as if one saw things, and the inclusion of noemata indicates not all phantasia cases require picture-like internal objects.
claims.warrant: Coherent sense can be made of the passages by focusing on 'appearing' without invoking pictorial images.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Thinking by itself is insufficient to lead to action; the object of thought must be present to awareness as an object of desire.
claims.ground: Aristotle insists on this in both DA III.9 and MA 6-7.
claims.warrant: Only once phantasia has endowed the object of perception with formal content can it become an object of pursuit or avoidance.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia ties abstract thought to concrete perceptible objects by providing the form to the noetic faculty.
claims.ground: Victory is regarded as desirable because we have an awareness of being superior; thought of victory is tied to the concrete impression of getting the better of some enemy.
claims.warrant: Such focusing on the concrete gives thought its motivating power; desire never has a purely abstract object.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Phantasia is introduced into thinking to maintain a consistently physicalist picture of action.
claims.ground: While thought processes are not necessarily accompanied by physiological change, in sublunary creatures every thought is accompanied by quasi-sensory awareness of the object's form, which is necessarily linked to physiological change.
claims.warrant: When judgment opposes sensory phantasia, the judgment cannot lead to action unless accompanied by a further activity of phantasia and hence physiological change.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: All thinking, theoretical as well as practical, is necessarily accompanied by some activity of phantasia.
claims.ground: There is no thinking that is simply abstract; every thought has some episode of symbolizing or envisaging that provides a concrete vehicle for the thought.
claims.warrant: One cannot think of a pure proposition; one must symbolize it by imagining an example, formalization, or saying words.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's theory that thinking requires phantasia is true as an empirical claim, though it might be falsified by discovery of purely abstract thinkers.
claims.ground: The theory is merely an empirical claim that could be upset by discovering people who think in purely abstract fashion.
claims.warrant: Empirical claims are validated or falsified by observational evidence.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle problematically suggests that phantasia activity is quasi-visual and involves picture-like objects that symbolize through similarity.
claims.ground: The triangle example uses the phrase 'he places before his eyes' and presents picturing and similarity as central cases.
claims.rebuttal: We have argued imaginings need not be definite and dense like pictures
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's trouble distinguishing phantasmata from prota noemata suggests he may not be deliberately restricting the account to the pictorial.
claims.ground: At the conclusion of DA III.8, Aristotle is troubled about how to distinguish phantasmata from prota noemata.
claims.warrant: If he were restricting the account to the pictorial, no such confusion would arise.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle's denial that thinking is physical commits him to a messy over-complexity requiring an extra phantasia in practical cases.
claims.ground: The thought of the sun's true size must be accompanied by symbolizing that is likely the same as the pre-judgmental phantasia seeing it as a foot wide, yet action theory forces insertion of an extra phantasia.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle could solve the over-complexity problem by adopting for thinking the functional account he gives for other life-processes, but good reasons prevent this.
claims.ground: There are good non-arbitrary reasons connected with his theory of action and responsibility that prevent adopting the view that thinking is a functional state of matter.
claims.rebuttal: These reasons have nothing to do with Platonist conservatism
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: The basic insight underlying Aristotle's phantasia theory is that perceptual reception is inseparable from interpretation.
claims.ground: We cannot explain an animal's perception of something as a distinct feature in his environment with reference only to receiving or imprinting, but must refer also to interpretive activity in virtue of which the scene appears a certain way to him.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Interpretive activity in perception depends on the creature's natural endowment, past, and other present activities.
claims.ground: Aristotle saw that this activity is dependent not only on natural endowment but also on past and other present activities.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: In explanation of action, the philosopher must begin with how the world looks to the particular creature, not with unprocessed sensory material.
claims.ground: Just as in science generally the philosopher must begin with and return to the phainomena (not 'pure' or 'raw' data), so in action explanation he must begin with the way the world looks to the creature.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Interest in appearing, not conviction that images play a central explanatory role, underlies Aristotle's development of phantasia theory.
claims.ground: This interest in appearing underlies his use of phantasia to explain apparently diverse happenings like imagination, dreaming, delusion, and motivation.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle is right not to make imaging theoretically central within his phantasia theory.
claims.ground: Because he does not make imaging central, his sub-theory of imaging is less objectionable than the blanket theory sometimes ascribed to him.
claims.rebuttal: Against the blanket theory sometimes ascribed to Aristotle
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Aristotle is right to make the same phantasia theory explain both practical and non-practical cases.
claims.ground: These differ not cognitively, but only with reference to the role played by desire.
claims.rebuttal: Against the mistaken notion that epistemology and explanation of action are two different branches of inquiry for Aristotle
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: To move a creature to action, an object must appear to him through selection, marking off, organization, and interpretation.
claims.ground: This is, desire aside, what it is to see the object.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action

claims.claim: Perception, thought, and action all presuppose the exercise of phantasia, not mere passive reception.
claims.ground: Learning to perceive is learning to make distinctions; the passive infant may receive stimuli, but perception, thought, and action presuppose exercise of phantasia.
claims.author: Nussbaum, Martha
claims.title: The Role of Phantasia in Aristotle's Explanation of Action
